transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I keep having nights where I eat way more than feels normal or safe. I’ll start with leftovers after grading papers, and then I’m eating cereal, crackers, peanut butter—whatever snacks I had packed for my classroom. It kind of scares me how much I can go through.
During these nighttime eating episodes, are you fully awake and aware of what you're doing, or do you often not remember them clearly afterward, as if you were half-asleep?
I’m not really sure what you mean by half-asleep. I know I eat a lot at night, but I haven’t really paid attention to whether I remember every part of it afterward.
During these nighttime eating episodes, do you feel like you can't stop eating or don't have control over how much you're consuming, even if you want to stop?
Yes. Once I start, it feels like the reasonable teacher part of me is saying, “Joan, stop,” but I just keep opening things and eating. I don’t feel like I can stop until I’m painfully full.
After these episodes of eating a lot at night, do you ever try to make up for it—like making yourself throw up, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising a lot—to avoid gaining weight?
Yes. The next day I’ll skip breakfast and lunch at school because I feel like I’m not allowed to eat. Then I’ll go hike for hours or do extra yoga, even when I’m shaky and exhausted.
Over the past few months, about how many times per week have these nighttime binge-eating episodes with the following restriction or excessive exercise been happening?

At least once a week, usually. There’s rarely been a week in the past few months where I don’t have one night like that, and then try to make up for it the next day by not eating or doing a long walk or extra yoga.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent episodes of eating an objectively large amount of food at night with a clear sense of loss of control, occurring at least once weekly for several months. These binge episodes are followed by compensatory behaviors—restrictive eating (skipping meals) and excessive exercise (prolonged hiking, extra yoga)—aimed at preventing weight gain.
